summary: This program defines a small reusable block of code called a method (Java's name for a function) and then runs it twice from main. It shows how naming a piece of work lets you repeat it without copying the code.

lines.text: Every Java program lives inside a class, and the class name here must match the file name IntroFunction.java.
This is the method Java looks for when it starts the program, so execution always begins on the first line inside it.
Calling the method by name hands control over to it; when the method finishes, the program returns here and continues with the next line.
The same call written a second time runs the method again, which is the whole point of putting the work in a method instead of repeating the print statement.
This declares the method: `void` means it hands nothing back to the caller, and the empty parentheses mean it needs no information to do its job.
This is the body of the method, the actual work that happens each time the method is called.
